transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Pierce (Redwood AE), Leah Ortiz (Redwood SE), Min Park (Redwood SE), Ravi Mehta (CTO - Atlasky), Sofia Alvarez (Platform Engineer - Atlasky), Evan Cole (SRE - Atlasky), Priya Nair (Product - Atlasky)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Redwood team walked Atlasky through org/project key patterns for multi-tenant rate controls, demoed Console rate governor UI and API examples, discussed dedicated vs hosted routing, and scoped a short POC. Key asks: sandbox tenant, sample traffic, security docs, pricing bands.

Topics covered:
- Org vs project key topologies
- Fairburst and sticky-routing policies
- Rate slicing and concurrency limits
- Console walkthrough: policy authoring + simulator
- API examples for token routing and fallback
- Security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Pierce: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through a 45-ish minute demo of our rate governor and org/project key playbook. Quick intros?
[00:12] Ravi Mehta: Hi, Ravi here, CTO at Atlasky. We build a commerce search layer, lots of multi-tenant traffic and spike patterns.
[00:18] Sofia Alvarez: Sofia, platform engineer, dealing with quotas and burst behavior.
[00:22] Evan Cole: Evan, SRE, I'll be focused on limits and fallbacks.
[00:27] Priya Nair: Priya from product, here to understand tradeoffs and customer UX.
[00:32] Jordan Pierce: Awesome. Leah and Min from our SE team will lead the console and traffic sim parts.
[00:36] Leah Ortiz: Hello all. Quick note, transcript might garble some proper nouns — KV cache sometimes comes out as K V cash — so please excuse that.

[02:05] Leah Ortiz: Ok, starting the Console. Top-left is org hierarchy; you can create projects and group keys. For Atlasky we'd suggest organization-level default quotas and then project keys per customer for fine-grained billing and burst control.
[02:44] Sofia Alvarez: Is there an easy migration path? We have an API key per tenant today in house, we'd like to map into Redwood org/project keys with minimal client work.
[03:02] Min Park: Yeah, you can do a transparent mapping — keep the same key on your side and create a project alias. We also support header-based routing if you can't change tokens immediately.
[03:25] Ravi Mehta: Latency matters for us. If we shard keys and route across dedicated pools, do we add hop or penalty?
[03:37] Leah Ortiz: Not really — routing is at the edge and policies are evaluated quickly. The tradeoff is choosing dedicated capacity (predictable throughput) vs hosted (cheaper, multi-tenant). For latency-critical endpoints we'd recommend dedicated model variants pinned to low-latency kernels.
[04:20] Evan Cole: Can we have sticky routing so certain VIP tenants always hit the same pool?
[04:28] Min Park: Yes, sticky lanes are supported. You can reserve lanes per project key and also set fallback lanes when a lane is saturated.

[06:00] Jordan Pierce: Let's talk quotas patterns. There are three we frequently recommend: org-defaults + project overrides, fairshare across projects, and burst fencing with leaky-bucket windows.
[06:20] Priya Nair: Break that down for product: what's a typical example?
[06:27] Leah Ortiz: Example: Org default 100 rps, project A has 50 guaranteed with 200 burst; project B 20 guaranteed with 80 burst; when overall capacity is constrained, the fairshare policy reduces non-guaranteed burst proportionally.
[07:03] Sofia Alvarez: Ok, and billing alignment — do we get token/time breakdowns per project key?
[07:14] Min Park: Yep, per-key metering with token-level cost attribution and traceable request IDs. Console shows top routes and cost heatmaps.

[09:10] Jordan Pierce: Now I'll flip to the policy simulator. You can upload a traffic trace and simulate policy effects. Leah, can you run the Atlasky sample we preloaded?
[09:22] Leah Ortiz: Running now — note this is a synthetic sample, not the customer CSV. Simulation shows a big spike at 03:12 with a VIP hitting 2k rps. Under org-defaults, that spike would push others down; with sticky lanes + reserved burst the VIP keeps steady at cost of using burst credits.
[10:05] Ravi Mehta: The simulator's numbers look optimistic — are those token approximations or measured?
[10:12] Min Park: They're estimated tokens per request; accuracy depends on prompt length variance. For accurate billing we recommend running a short real-traffic POC.

[12:30] Evan Cole: Security — we need SOC2 and encryption at rest with customer KMS. Also audit logs and SSO via SAML.
[12:42] Jordan Pierce: We have SOC2 Type II, support KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments, and SSO/SAML plus RBAC in the Console. We'll attach the security pack.
[13:01] Sofia Alvarez: For on-prem or VPC, is the control plane still Redwood managed?
[13:08] Leah Ortiz: In VPC mode, control plane is customer-visible; for air-gapped we offer a private deployment package. Audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM.

[15:00] Priya Nair: One concern: if we throttle aggressively, UX might degrade. Any graceful degradation patterns?
[15:10] Min Park: Yes — Redwood supports staged degrade: a) return low-confidence fallback responses, b) async queueing for non-critical requests, c) redirect to a cheaper model variant. You can configure these as route-level fallbacks.
[15:50] Ravi Mehta: How do we test fallback behavior automatically?
[15:55] Leah Ortiz: We have a canary and rollout feature integrated with traffic-splitting. You can run a canary that sends 5% traffic through fallback policies and measure latency/error delta.

[18:30] Jordan Pierce: Let's switch to the API demo — token routing via header x-reddy-project-key (note: header name is an example).
[18:40] Min Park: Example curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer RED_KEY' -H 'X-Project-Key: atlasky-tenant-123' -d '{"prompt":"..."}' The platform resolves the key and applies project policies.
[19:15] Sofia Alvarez: If we keep our existing key material, can we do a mapping layer instead of issuing new tokens?
[19:22] Min Park: Yes, mapping layer at the edge or a quick rewrite in API gateway. We demonstrated header mapping earlier.

[21:05] Evan Cole: In a failure scenario where dedicated pool is down, how immediate is the fallback to hosted?
[21:12] Leah Ortiz: Fallback is immediate per routing policy. You can define automatic fallback to a compatible model variant in a different pool or region; it can be synchronous with minimal retries.
[21:40] Ravi Mehta: What about cold starts with large models? We saw variability with other vendors.
[21:48] Min Park: Our serving runtime pre-warms kernels for pinned variants and does KV cache warming for hot prompts. Cold starts are minimized for dedicated pools — still some cost tradeoff.

[24:00] Jordan Pierce: Pricing question: how does burst consumption affect billing for dedicated vs hosted?
[24:09] Leah Ortiz: Hosted is pay-per-token with burst usage billed normally. For Dedicated, you have committed capacity; burst beyond committed is billed as overage. We can show pricing bands after the call.
[24:35] Priya Nair: Any SLA differences tied to model variants?
[24:40] Min Park: SLA is attached to the Dedicated offering and to pinned model sets; hosted has best-effort latency targets and usage guards.

[27:00] Leah Ortiz: Walkthrough of Optimize suggestions: the tool recommends batching settings, quantization profiles, and pre-tokenization to save token costs while staying within latency SLOs.
[27:22] Sofia Alvarez: Do these recommendations come with estimated cost delta?
[27:26] Leah Ortiz: Yes, Optimize shows % cost savings and expected latency impact. There are simulation modes too.

[30:00] Jordan Pierce: Let's hit some edge cases — multi-tenant burst when a single customer misbehaves and then goes quiet. How do we prevent cascading backpressure?
[30:10] Min Park: We recommend a three-layer approach: immediate per-key hard limit, per-project soft limit with adaptive backoff, and org-level circuit breaker. Adaptive backoff reduces the client's allowed rate gradually instead of a hard cut.
[31:00] Evan Cole: Could adaptive backoff be exploited by a noisy neighbor that just keeps reconnecting?
[31:05] Leah Ortiz: We have sticky counters and anomaly detection; repeated reconnects get classified as abusive and can be moved to a quarantine lane with stricter limits.

[33:20] Ravi Mehta: For the POC, we'd like to validate: 1) routing correctness across keys, 2) simulator vs real traffic alignment, 3) secure comms and audit logs.
[33:32] Jordan Pierce: That aligns with our usual POC scope. We'll provision a sandbox tenant, you'll send a 48h traffic dump, we'll run the simulator and then run a small live test with a throttled slice.
[34:10] Priya Nair: How invasive is the integration for our frontend clients?
[34:17] Min Park: Minimal — mostly header/token changes or a simple gateway rewrite. We can provide middleware snippets for common platforms.

[36:00] Sofia Alvarez: Any known gotchas? For us, auth rotation and key compromise are concerns — rotating keys without impacting an active session.
[36:10] Leah Ortiz: We support key rotation with grace windows; old tokens can be accepted for a configurable period and shadow mode to confirm mapping.

[38:50] Jordan Pierce: Quick live demo: Leah will create a project key, set a 100 rps limit with 300 burst, and we hit it with a small load generator.
[39:05] Leah Ortiz: Creating key now... done. Setting policy and starting load. You'll see in the console the token-level metrics, the drop in allowed rate and the simulated fallback to a smaller model variant.
[40:00] Evan Cole: I see a spike and then a queued backlog indicator — nice. The logs show request IDs and which fallback triggered.
[40:25] Min Park: Logs are exportable to your SIEM. Also, we store a compact request trace for 30 days by default; retention is configurable.

[42:30] Ravi Mehta: Curious — any customers in retail or commerce who've used sticky lanes and seen measurable latency improvements?
[42:38] Jordan Pierce: Yes, a couple of commerce customers reported 20-40% latency tail improvements by reserving lanes for checkout flows. We'll share anonymized case notes.

[44:00] Jordan Pierce: Quick recap and next steps: Jordan to send playbook and pricing, Leah to provision sandbox and demo scripts, Atlasky to share 48h traffic and whitelist IPs, schedule POC kickoff.
[44:20] Priya Nair: That sounds good. Also, can you include an appendix on fallback UX recommendations for product?
[44:26] Jordan Pierce: Yes, we'll include best-practice doc.
[45:00] Sofia Alvarez: One last question — how long to get Dedicated pool live?
[45:06] Min Park: Typically 2-6 weeks depending on capacity and contractual lead time; sandbox can be ready in 48 hours.
[45:30] Jordan Pierce: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials.
[45:40] Ravi Mehta: Thanks — appreciate the walkthrough.

End of transcript.
